title: GLUT: 3D Gaussian Lookup Table for Continuous Color Transformation
claim: Grid-based and black-box neural representations each have limits; ours uses explicit continuous primitives that are compact and interpretable.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right, zoomed inset on final panel
description: Three side-by-side panels compare ways to represent a color transformation, each with an RGB axis cue. (a) Traditional LUT: a cube with a regular lattice of dots colored by their RGB value, plus a 'LUT data' legend. (b) INR-based LUT: a small fully connected neural network with R, G, B input nodes on the left and R', G', B' outputs on the right, drawn as gray circles and dense lines. (c) Gaussian LUT (ours): a cube holding several translucent purple ellipsoids. A dashed zoom inset shows one Gaussian with its center, covariance, opacity colorbar from 0 to 1, a point x mapped by an affine function, and a formula. Captions sit below each panel. The eye goes first to the colorful grid, then to the purple ellipsoids and the inset.
caption: Comparison between different color LUT representations. (a) Explicit Traditional LUT vs. (b) Implicit INR-based LUT vs. (c) Explicit Gaussian LUT (Ours).
abstract: 3D Lookup Tables (3D LUTs) are widely used for color mapping, but their grid-based representation discretizes the RGB space, leading to a capacity-memory trade-off that becomes prohibitive when storing large numbers of LUTs. Recent approaches use implicit neural representations to improve scalability, but their black-box nature limits interpretability and localized editing. In this paper, we propose Gaussian LUT (GLUT), a continuous and explicit representation of color transformations using learnable 3D Gaussian primitives. By eliminating fixed-resolution grids, GLUT provides flexible representational capacity with a compact memory footprint. Its spatially localized primitives also facilitate interpretation and targeted editing. Building on GLUT, we introduce Conditional Gaussian LUT (CGLUT), a compact generator that predicts GLUT parameters for multiple LUTs within a shared framework, enabling smooth blending between color styles. GLUT further supports efficient local editing by allowing targeted adjustments to specific color regions without retraining the model. Experiments show that GLUT outperforms existing neural LUT representations in both accuracy and efficiency, while supporting controllable localized color editing. CGLUT further improves compact modeling and smooth blending of multiple color styles. Code is available at https://github.com/CVC-Color/glut.
